title: Developer Experience: SDK Guides, Quickstarts, API Examples and Top Support Fixes (Playbook)
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Overview:

This playbook describes the Developer Experience (DevEx) documentation standard for SDK guides, quickstarts and templates, API examples, docs-site operating procedures, and the canonical fixes for top support issues. It is intended for content authors, SDK owners, DevRel, and support engineers. The goal is to ensure consistent, reliable, and discoverable docs that reduce time-to-first-success and lower support load.

Scope:

- SDK guides: Python, JavaScript/TS, Go, and CLI examples.
- Quickstarts and templates: minimal reproducible steps for common integrations (text generation, chat, embeddings, reranking).
- API examples: curl and SDK-first patterns including streaming and function/tool calling.
- Docs site operating procedures: authoring, review, publishing, versioning, and rollout.
- Top support issues: triage patterns and canonical fixes for the five most frequent issues reported by support.

Ownership and roles:

- Author: initial writer (usually SDK owner or DevRel).
- Reviewer(s): at least one SDK owner and one support engineer.
- Approver: DevEx manager for cross-team content; security reviewer for any data-handling guidance.
- Maintainer: SDK or product owner responsible for keeping examples accurate with SDK releases.

Doc templates and inventory (minimum required sections for each doc):

1) Title (short, hyphenated file name)
2) One-line summary
3) Audience and prerequisites (required API keys, account settings, rate limits)
4) Quickstart (5-10 minute path)
5) Detailed examples (sync, async/streaming, error handling)
6) Troubleshooting / Common errors
7) Links: SDK repo, package registry, changelog, related Confluence pages
8) Ownership and last updated date

Example quickstart template (text):

- Prereqs:
  - Redwood API key with dev scope
  - Python 3.10+ / Node 18+ / Go 1.20+
  - Virtual environment (recommended)
- Steps:
  1) pip install redwood-sdk  # or npm install @redwood/inference
  2) export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-...
  3) python quickstart_generate.py  # example script included in repo
- Verify:
  - Response contains generated text and cost/latency headers

Canonical SDK guide structure (example headings to include):

- Introduction and use cases
- Authentication and configuration
- Simple requests (sync)
- Streaming responses and cancellation
- Function/tool calling example
- Error handling and retry guidance (idempotency keys for non-idempotent ops)
- Performance tips (batching, caching, sequence-length controls)
- Tests and CI checks for examples

API examples (must include both curl and SDK):

Curl example - text generation:

curl -sS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate \
  -d '{"model":"redwood-alpha-1","input":"Write an onboarding checklist for a new engineer."}'

Python SDK example (sync):

from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key="${REDWOOD_API_KEY}")
resp = client.generate(model="redwood-alpha-1", input="Summarize this product doc in two bullets")
print(resp.text)

JavaScript SDK example (streaming):

import Redwood from '@redwood/inference';
const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
const stream = await client.generateStream({ model: 'redwood-alpha-1', input: 'Explain caching strategies for LLMs' });
for await (const chunk of stream) { console.log(chunk.text); }

Docs site operating procedures (authoring -> publish):

Authoring checklist:
- Use the doc template; confirm audience and prerequisites.
- Confirm code samples run locally and in CI (we run smoke tests for Python/JS snippets).
- Add labels: sdk, quickstart, stable|experimental, language (python/js/go).
- Add related_pages links and an owner.

Review process:
- Create a doc PR in docs repo with the Confluence export artifact.
- Tag reviewers: SDK owner + support engineer.
- Resolve technical comments and update code samples.
- Security review required if doc contains data handling or KMS instructions.

Publishing steps:
1) Merge doc PR to docs/main. CI runs snippet tests and link-checker.
2) DevEx engineer runs site build and smoke test in staging: /staging/docs.
3) Run broken-link-check and search-index update (script: scripts/update_search_index.sh).
4) Publish to prod and announce on #devex-docs with summary and changed pages.

Versioning and compatibility:
- Tag SDK examples with SDK version used (example: Python v1.4.0).
- For breaking API changes, keep archived examples under /archive/<version> and add deprecation notices.
- Use labels stable|experimental to guide readers.

Monitoring and maintenance:
- Weekly doc triage: triage new support tickets referencing docs and apply fixes within 5 business days for high-impact issues.
- Monthly audits: run snippet smoke tests for top-50 pages.
- Errors found in examples trigger a bug label and assign to SDK owner for patch.

Top support issues and canonical fixes (current most-frequent):

1) Issue: Authentication errors (401/403)
   - Symptom: Requests return 401 or 403, or responses contain "invalid_api_key".
   - Root causes:
     - Missing/expired API key in environment
     - Incorrect header format (e.g. using X-Api-Key instead of Authorization Bearer)
   - Canonical fix steps:
     1) Verify environment: echo $REDWOOD_API_KEY
     2) Check header: must be Authorization: Bearer <key>
     3) If using CI, ensure secrets are present for the runner and not redacted in logs.
   - Verification: curl to /v1/health returns 200 when authorized.
   - Owner: SDK owner / identity team

2) Issue: High latency or timeouts on generation requests
   - Symptom: Long tail latency > SLO (p95 > 500ms for short prompts) or client side timeouts.
   - Root causes:
     - Wrong model selected for expected latency profile (use low-latency model for chat)
     - Large batch sizes or unbounded max_tokens
     - Regional routing to a busy zone
   - Canonical fix steps:
     1) Recommend model with low-latency profile in docs and quickstarts (e.g., redwood-alpha-lowlatency).
     2) Set sensible client timeout (30s default in SDK samples) and max_tokens limits.
     3) Check request region and retry to another endpoint if supported.
   - Verification: Re-run example and measure x-request-latency header.
   - Owner: runtime/perf team + SDK owner

3) Issue: Streaming connections drop unexpectedly
   - Symptom: Partial output, connection closed, or "broken pipe" errors.
   - Root causes:
     - Client does not handle chunked transfer properly.
     - Intermediate proxies (corporate proxies) closing idle connections.
   - Canonical fix steps:
     1) Use the SDK streaming client (it handles reconnection/cancelation semantics).
     2) If using raw HTTP, ensure Transfer-Encoding: chunked is supported and read until stream terminator.
     3) Recommend keep-alive and periodic heartbeats for long streams.
   - Verification: Run streaming sample in local env and in corporate network.
   - Owner: SDK owner + networking team

4) Issue: Incorrect or unexpected outputs when using function/tool calling
   - Symptom: Model ignores the tool schema or returns free text instead of JSON.
   - Root causes:
     - Mismatch between declared function schema and tool input types.
     - Missing deterministic prompts and examples for the function behavior.
   - Canonical fix steps:
     1) Confirm function JSON schema matches the payload sent in examples.
     2) Add explicit examples and a short instruction to prefer JSON output.
     3) Add post-validation step in client to reject non-conforming outputs and fallback to a safe path.
   - Verification: Run function-calling test harness in evals and assert schema compliance.
   - Owner: applied-ml-and-evals + SDK owner

5) Issue: Embeddings mismatch (different similarity results across SDKs)
   - Symptom: Same input returns different vectors length or different near-neighbor rankings in Python vs JS.
   - Root causes:
     - Different tokenization libraries or pre/post-processing steps in SDKs.
     - Using different model variants (float32 vs quantized) without documented differences.
   - Canonical fix steps:
     1) Confirm SDKs use the same tokenizer and pre-processing (document exact tokenizer version).
     2) Add deterministic test vectors and a small CI job that verifies embedding similarity across SDKs.
     3) Document known differences for quantized variants.
   - Verification: Run cross-language test and compare cosine similarity thresholds.
   - Owner: embeddings team + SDK owners

Troubleshooting commands and utilities (examples):
- Healthcheck: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/health
- Inspect headers: curl -I -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_API_KEY" https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate -d '{}'
- Check logs (GKE example): kubectl -n redwood logs deployment/redwood-runtime -c runtime --since=10m | grep ERROR
- Run snippet tests: ./scripts/run_snippet_smoke_tests.sh --languages python,js

Change log and release notes guidance:
- Every docs change that updates code samples must include a "Tested with" line (SDK version and date).
- For breaking changes, include migration steps and code diffs.

Appendix: Example CI snippet for snippet smoke tests (bash):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
./scripts/run_snippet_smoke_tests.sh --languages python js || { echo 'Snippet tests failed'; exit 1; }

Contacts and escalation:
- DevEx on-call: #devex-oncall (pager duty)
- Support escalation: support-leads@redwood.ai
- Security review: security-review@redwood.ai

Related artifacts and repositories:
- SDKs: github.com/redwood-ai/sdk-python, sdk-js, sdk-go
- Docs repo: github.com/redwood-ai/docs
- Evals: confluence/agents (see applied-ml-and-evals/eval-harness)

This playbook should be revisited quarterly or after any major SDK or API change. For suggestions or corrections, open a PR in the docs repo and tag the reviewers listed above.
